title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 11
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Crop That Changed a Continent
passages.text:
A. The movement of crops between continents after the fifteenth century altered diets, populations and landscapes more profoundly than the movement of people that carried them. Maize, cassava, tomatoes, chillies and the potato travelled in one direction; wheat, rice, sugar and coffee in the other. What followed was not a straightforward improvement but a reorganisation whose winners and losers were determined by soil, climate and land tenure rather than by the merits of the plants.

B. The potato's advantage over the grains it competed with was arithmetic. It yields more calories per unit of land, tolerates poor and acidic soils, requires no milling or threshing, and can be left in the ground until needed. On smallholdings too small to feed a family on grain, it made subsistence possible where it had not been, and the population increases that followed its adoption in several regions are among the clearest demonstrations available that food supply and population are linked.

C. Adoption was nonetheless slow and the resistance was not simple ignorance. The plant was unfamiliar, belonged to a family containing known poisons, and produced no seed that farmers recognised. More practically, it did not fit existing arrangements: rents were assessed in grain, tithes were levied on grain, and a crop that could be left underground was harder for a landlord or tax collector to observe and value. Cultivators had reasons beyond conservatism to hesitate.

D. The same properties that made the crop valuable made the systems built on it fragile. Potatoes were propagated from tubers rather than seed, so a region's crop could be genetically near-identical, and a pathogen defeating one plant's defences defeated the whole. Where a population had come to depend on a single crop grown as effectively a single variety, the arrival of a disease it could not resist produced famine on a scale that the same disease in a diverse system would not have caused.

E. Blaming the failure on the plant is a persistent error. Regions growing the same crop with the same pathogen present suffered very differently, and the difference tracked land ownership, the availability of alternative food, and whether food continued to be exported during shortage. The biological event was necessary and not sufficient; what converted a crop failure into mass mortality was the arrangement of entitlement to food, and that lesson has been repeatedly relearned in later famines.

F. The response, once understood, was genetic rather than agronomic. Collecting and maintaining the wild relatives and traditional varieties of a crop preserves resistance traits that commercial breeding has narrowed away, and every subsequent defence against potato disease has drawn on material from the crop's region of origin. This is the practical argument for conserving diversity that is no longer planted, and it is stronger than the aesthetic one usually offered.

passages.title: Out of Step
passages.text:
Living things time their activities to the year, and the cues they use are not the same. Some species respond to day length, which is fixed and unchanging from year to year. Others respond to temperature, which is not. For most of evolutionary history this difference did not matter, because temperature and day length were reliably correlated. As average temperatures have risen, the correlation has weakened, and species using different cues have begun to shift by different amounts.

The consequence is mismatch. A caterpillar that emerges when oak leaves appear, and a bird that times breeding so that chicks hatch when caterpillars are abundant, form a chain whose links respond to different signals. Where the plant and the insect advance with warmth and the bird advances less, because its cue is partly photoperiodic, the peak food supply arrives before the peak demand. The birds are not late in any absolute sense; they are late relative to a resource that moved.

Measuring this requires records longer than most ecological studies, which is why much of the evidence comes from unusual sources. Datasets kept by amateur naturalists over decades, estate records of first flowering, and log books of migration arrival dates have provided the time depth that funded research programmes rarely achieve. The reliance on such records is a strength in duration and a weakness in standardisation, and analyses generally spend considerable effort establishing that apparent trends are not artefacts of who was recording and how.

The effects are uneven in a way that complicates simple predictions. Species with flexible timing, broad diets or multiple broods absorb mismatch relatively well. Specialists dependent on a narrow window suffer disproportionately, and long-distance migrants are structurally disadvantaged because the cue available to them — conditions in a wintering area thousands of kilometres away — carries no information about conditions at the destination. Some populations have adjusted through shifts in the timing of departure; others have not, and the difference between them is an active question rather than a settled one.

Evolutionary adjustment is possible and its speed is the central uncertainty. Timing is heritable, selection against mistimed individuals is measurable, and documented shifts in the genetic basis of timing exist in a small number of well-studied populations. Whether such adjustment can occur fast enough depends on generation length, population size and the rate of environmental change, and confident statements in either direction outrun the evidence.

What the field has established firmly is narrower than the popular account. Phenologies are shifting, they are shifting at different rates, and mismatches have been demonstrated in specific well-documented systems. The general claim that ecosystems are unravelling through mistiming is plausible, poorly quantified at scale, and rests on extrapolation from a small number of intensively studied cases in a limited number of habitats.

passages.title: The Experiment That Would Not Repeat
passages.text:
A published scientific result carries an implicit claim: that an appropriately equipped stranger following the described method would obtain a comparable outcome. Systematic attempts to test that claim, beginning in the 2010s across several disciplines, produced replication rates substantially lower than researchers had expected — a finding that generated a period of institutional alarm and a more useful period of analysis.

The initial framing as a crisis of misconduct was almost entirely wrong. Fabrication exists and is rare, and it accounts for very little of the failure to replicate. What the analysis identified instead were ordinary practices, individually defensible, which collectively inflate the rate of false positives: analysing data before deciding when to stop collecting it, choosing among several outcome measures after seeing the results, excluding cases by criteria formed during analysis, and reporting the comparisons that reached significance among many that were run.

None of these requires intent to deceive, and that is the important point. A researcher making each choice can offer a sound justification for it, and the problem lies in the flexibility of the sequence rather than in any single decision. Where many defensible analytical paths exist and the one reported is selected partly because of what it produced, the reported statistical result no longer means what it appears to mean, and the researcher may be entirely unaware of the process.

Publication practice compounded this structurally. Journals preferred novel positive findings, replications were difficult to publish, and null results frequently went unwritten. The literature therefore represented not the set of experiments conducted but a filtered subset, and any reader estimating the strength of evidence from published papers was working from a sample selected on the outcome being estimated. This is not a subtle bias; it is a fundamental one, and it was widely known and long tolerated.

The reforms adopted address the mechanism rather than exhorting researchers to be careful. Pre-registration fixes the analysis plan before data are seen, which removes the flexibility that produced the problem. Registered reports have journals accept a study on the basis of its question and method before results exist, which removes the incentive to produce a particular outcome. Data and code sharing allows a stranger to check the path from observation to conclusion. Adoption is partial, uneven between fields, and where measured has raised replication rates.

The episode is often narrated as a failure and is better read as a success of the ordinary kind. A discipline examined its own output, found a defect, identified its mechanism, and changed its procedures — which is what the scientific method is supposed to do and what its critics frequently claim it does not. The finding that many published results are unreliable came from science, not from its detractors, and the appropriate response is neither dismissal of the literature nor confidence that the problem is now solved.
